directional_or_weak_substitution_warning.excerpt: APWP for the block was presented by Lin (1984) based on the results of his large-scale paleomagnetic study of China. Since then, more poles for the Yangtze Block have been published, with some of the most reliable results coming from the Mesozoic (e.g. Linet al., 1985; Opdyke et al., 1986; Heller et al., 1988; Steiner et al., 1989). The most recent and comprehensive APWP for Yangtze from the Permian to the Present, was published by Enkin et al. (1992), incorporating and critically evaluating the results to date. The problems of remagnetization and working in a tectonically disturbed area, however, have hampered refinement of the APWP for this block. Although the Mesozoic has been studied in perhaps the most detail - the Triassic in particular - there are still few reliable poles reported in the literature. This scarcity of reported poles for south China from the Mesozoic and large statistical ambiguities have resulted in an APWP with large confidence limits in which the trend of the pole path is emerging but the detail is still lacking. The most recent and comprehensive APWP for Yangtze from the Permian to the Present, was published by Enkin et al. (1992), incorporating and critically evaluating the results to date. The problems of remagnetization and working in a tectonically disturbed area, however, have hampered refinement of the APWP for this block. Although the Mesozoic has been studied in perhaps the most detail - the Triassic in particular - there are still few reliable poles reported in the literature. This scarcity of reported poles for south China from the Mesozoic and large statistical ambiguities have resulted in an APWP with large confidence limits in which the trend of the pole path is emerging but the detail is still lacking. The large A95 of the Middle to Late Triassic pole position (Enkin et al., 1992), however, and the recent discrepancies of Triassic results for the Yangtze Block (Steiner et al., 1989; Dobson and Heller, 1993) mean that a post-folding, Middle to Late Triassic remagnetization should not be completely ruled out. The question then arises - why are the Yinkeng sediments apparently unaffected by the remagnetization that affected the Changxing Formation? Results of the IRM studies reveal that the only significant difference in the magnetic minerals from the two formations is the presence of goethite in the Yinkeng Formation. There is evidence for the presence of magnetite as well as hematite in both formations, though the relative abundances and grain sizes may play a role in the stability of the signals. The overlapping of the blocking temperature spectra, however, make it difficult to determine the relative contributions of each (Figure 4). All of the stable Yinkeng samples come from the dolomitic layers in the section, while the samples from the Changxing Formation and the unstable Yinkeng samples come from limestones. All of the stable Yinkeng samples come from the dolomitic layers in the section, while the samples from the Changxing Formation and the unstable Yinkeng samples come from limestones. The only difference seen in the IRM experiments between the dolomites and limestones is reflected in the presence of goethite in the dolomites. Its origin is unclear. It seems then, that the dolomitization of these sediments may be responsible for the preservation of the Early Triassic magnetization since the formation of dolomite can, in many cases, greatly decrease the porosity of a rock unit. This reduction in porosity may have prevented fluids responsible for the Jurassic remagnetization events from passing through the dolomite, thus enabling the preservation of the Early Triassic signal in those sediments. Paleomagnetic and rock magnetic experiments on the Triassic Yinkeng Formation and the Permian Changxing Formation sampled from the Permian-Triassic type section, Changxing County, reveal that a high temperature primary direction is isolated in dolomitic samples from the Early Triassic but the Late Permian limestones samples appear to be remagnetized during the Jurassic. A Permian-Triassic pole previously reported for the Changxing Formation from this section (Linet al., 1985) is not in agreement with results from this study or other poles for that time interval reported for the Yangtze Block and may be remagnetized. Introduction The Changxing Permian-Triassic type section is located in the Baoqing Quarry, Changxing County, about 80 km north of Hangzhou (Figure 1). Exposed in the quarry is 50 meters of irregularly bedded greyish limestones with some inte

(Figure 1). Exposed in the quarry is 50 meters of irregularly bedded greyish limestones with some interbedded grey mudstones and shales, and dolomites and limestones in the late part of the Yinkeng Formation. The boundary between the Late Permian Changxing Formation and the Early Triassic Yinkeng is marked by a greyish- yellowish boundary clay layer. The section was sampled by Lin and others (1985) and the results were used in the calculation of a Permian-Triassic pole for the Yangtze Block. This section was also sampled by Li and Wang (1987) and they were able to resolve a magnetic stratigraphy though Lin (1984) reported only one polarity from the section. Recently it has been shown that Lin's pole from the Changxing section may be remagnetized (Steiner et al., 1989; Dobson and Mauritsch, 1989). In the most recent and comprehensive compilation of Chinese results from the Permian to Present, Enkin et al. (1992) use the results from 16 samples at the very top of this section (from the study of Li and Wang) in calculations of a mean Early Triassic paleopole for the Yangtze Block. Introduction The Changxing Permian-Triassic type section is located in the Baoqing Quarry, Changxing County, about 80 km north of Hangzhou (Figure 1). Exposed in the quarry is 50 meters of irregularly bedded greyish limestones with some interbedded grey mudstones and shales, and dolomites and limestones in the late part of the Yinkeng Formation. The boundary between the Late Permian Changxing Formation and the Early Triassic Yinkeng is marked by a greyish- yellowish boundary clay layer. This section was also sampled by Li and Wang (1987) and they were able to resolve a magnetic stratigraphy though Lin (1984) reported only one polarity from the section. These were the only results from outside of the south-central Sichuan Province area used by Enkin et al. (1992) in the calculation of the Early Triassic direction for the block and are, therefore, very important. For this reason, we present here new results from our study of the Changxing section and examine the rock magnetic properties of samples from the section. sition (33.0øN, 193.8øE) falls off of the APWP. The large A95 of the Middle to Late Triassic pole position (Enkin et al., 1992), however, and the recent discrepancies of Triassic results for the Yangtze Block (Steiner et al., 1989; Dobson and Heller, 1993) mean that a post-folding, Middle to Late Triassic remagnetization should not be completely ruled out. The question then arises - why are the Yinkeng sediments apparently unaffected by the remagnetization that affected the Changxing Formation? Results of the IRM studies reveal that the only significant difference in the magnetic minerals from the two formations is the presence of goethite in the Yinkeng Formation. There is evidence for the presence of magnetite as well as hematite in both formations, though the relative abundances and grain sizes may play a role in the stability of the signals. The overlapping of the blocking temperature spectra, however, make it difficult to determine the relative contributions of each (Figure 4). All of the stable Yinkeng samples come from the dolomitic layers in the section, while the samples from the Changxing Formation and the unstable Yinkeng samples come from limestones. The overlapping of the blocking temperature spectra, however, make it difficult to determine the relative contributions of each (Figure 4). All of the stable Yinkeng samples come from the dolomitic layers in the section, while the samples from the Changxing Formation and the unstable Yinkeng samples come from limestones. The only difference seen in the IRM experiments between the dolomites and limestones is reflected in the presence of goethite in the dolomites. Its origin is unclear. It seems then, that the dolomitization of these sediments may be responsible for the preservation of the Early Triassic magnetization since the formation of dolomite can, in many cases, greatly decrease the porosity of a rock unit. This reduction in porosity may have prevented fluids responsible for the Jurassic remagnetization events from passing through the dolomite, thus enabling the preservation of the Early Triassic signal in those sediments. Earth Sci. 30, 776-786 (1993) Objectives Paleomagnetic studies have been carried out on red sand- stone beds exposed on either side of Lourdes Cove, Port au Port peninsula, in western Newfoundland. The objectives of the studies were threefold. The first objective was to contrib- ute to the data base for western Newfoundland that provides evidence of various motions involved in the closing of the Iapetus Ocean during the Paleozoic. The geology of the island of Newfoundland has been interpreted over the past 25 years as resulting from the opening and closing of an early Paleozoic Iapetus Ocean (Wilson 1966; Williams et al. 1972; Williams 1979 and references therein; McKerrow and Scotese 1990; Williams 1992). Apart from the rotations of western New- foundland relative to cratonic North America that were sug- Printed in Canada / Imprimt au Canada gested by Black (1964), western Newfoundland has always been considered part of cratonic North America. A compari- son of western Newfoundland paleomagnetic data with data of contemporaneous rocks from Avalonia would provide reason- able constraints on the suggested motions at the time of the closing of the Iapetus Ocean. The second objective was to establish whether the red sand- stone units on eithe

Four distinct lithotectonic zones were recognized; from west to east, these were the Humber, Dunnage, Gander, and Avalon zones. The Port au Port Penin- sula, in the Humber Zone, has been extensively studied geo- logically (Schuchert and Dunbar 1934; Sullivan 1940; Riley 1962; Rodgers and Neale 1963; Rodgers 1965; Fahraeus 1973; O'Brien 1975; Dean 1979; Williams 1985). interest in the present study are the coastal exposures of red sandstones between Misty Point and Red Point on either side of Lourdes Cove (Fig. 1). In most of the literature cited above, they are described as part of the Clam Bank Formation. They comprise mostly brick-red sandstone and mudstone. The sandstones exhibit cross-bedding and are commonly coarse grained. Units of fine-grained sandstone and siltstone alternate with mudstone and coarse-grained sand- stone. At the north end of Lourdes Cove, rocks of the Clam Bank Formation conformably overlie the grey sandstones of the Middle Ordovician Long Point Group (Rodgers 1965; Williams 1985). At the south end of Lourdes Cove, Rodgers (1965) recognized Siluro-Devonian brachiopods in grey shales and sandstones of the Clam Bank Formation. Along Long Point, the Clam Bank Formation and the upper member of the Long Point Group are homoclinal. Strata of the two forma- tions strike at approximately 240" and dip at 40-50" NW. From about 2 km northeast of Lourdes to Red Point, all expo- sures dip southeast, sometimes by as much as 80". Earth Sci. 30, 776-786 (1993) Objectives Paleomagnetic studies have been carried out on red sand- stone beds exposed on either side of Lourdes Cove, Port au Port peninsula, in western Newfoundland. The objectives of the studies were threefold. The first objective was to contrib- ute to the data base for western Newfoundland that provides evidence of various motions involved in the closing of the Iapetus Ocean during the Paleozoic. The geology of the island of Newfoundland has been interpreted over the past 25 years as resulting from the opening and closing of an early Paleozoic Iapetus Ocean (Wilson 1966; Williams et al. 1972; Williams 1979 and references therein; McKerrow and Scotese 1990; Williams 1992). Apart from the rotations of western New- foundland relative to cratonic North America that were sug- Printed in Canada / Imprimt au Canada gested by Black (1964), western Newfoundland has always been considered part of cratonic North America. A compari- son of western Newfoundland paleomagnetic data with data of contemporaneous rocks from Avalonia would provide reason- able constraints on the suggested motions at the time of the closing of the Iapetus Ocean. The second objective was to establish whether the red sand- stone units on eithe

interest in the present study are the coastal exposures of red sandstones between Misty Point and Red Point on either side of Lourdes Cove (Fig. 1). In most of the literature cited above, they are described as part of the Clam Bank Formation. They comprise mostly brick-red sandstone and mudstone. The sandstones exhibit cross-bedding and are commonly coarse grained. Units of fine-grained sandstone and siltstone alternate with mudstone and coarse-grained sand- stone. At the north end of Lourdes Cove, rocks of the Clam Bank Formation conformably overlie the grey sandstones of the Middle Ordovician Long Point Group (Rodgers 1965; Williams 1985). At the south end of Lourdes Cove, Rodgers (1965) recognized Siluro-Devonian brachiopods in grey shales and sandstones of the Clam Bank Formation. Along Long Point, the Clam Bank Formation and the upper member of the Long Point Group are homoclinal. Strata of the two forma- tions strike at approximately 240" and dip at 40-50" NW. From about 2 km northeast of Lourdes to Red Point, all expo- sures dip southeast, sometimes by as much as 80". The dominant down-west mag- netization was described in a number of studies including Strangway (1961), Fahrig et al. A second rernanence (herein called the Senneterre remanence) has been reported in the literature at only four sites. It was recognized as an up-north magnetization by Larochelle (1966) at three sampling sites in two dykes, and as a magnetization of opposite polarity by Symons et al. (1981) at a single site. Preliminary unpublished work (W.F. Fahrig, personal com- munication 1985) indicated that this magnetization occurs in other northeast-trending quartz tholeiite ,dykes. The first component removed is usually a minor secondary mag- netization of northerly declination and moderate positive incli- nation and is aligned approximately subparallel with the Earth's present field direction. This magnetization is com- monly removed by AF demagnetization of 5 - 10 mT and by thermal demagnetization in temperatures less than 300°C. Plagioclase and clinopyroxene (augite) are the domi- nant primary phases, but some sills contain up to 5 - 10% oli- vine or quartz and potassium-feldspar in graphic intergrowths. Granophyric zones have been reported from some sills (Shride 1967). Accessory phases include minor biotite and hornblende and the opaque phases magnetite, ilmenite, and sulfides (pyrite, chalcopyrite, and pyrrhotite). The diabase sheets are commonly partially to completely altered and replaced by secondary phases. Olivine, where originally present, is altered to serpentine and magnetite, or talc, iddingsite, or bowlingite. Pyroxene is altered to blue-green amphibole and chlorite, or uralite, whereas plagioclase is replaced by clay minerals or carbonate, epidote, and clinozoisite (Shride 1967; Smith 1970; Banks and Krieger 1977). The alteration is thought to be largely deuteric in origin and not the result of subsequent metamorphic, hydrothermal, or tectonothermal events (Shride 1967; Smith 1970; Wrucke 1989; Hammond and Wooden 1990). Most samples contained one or two magnetic components. The first component removed is usually a minor secondary mag- netization of northerly declination and moderate positive incli- nation and is aligned approximately subparallel with the Earth's present field direction. This magnetization is com- monly removed by AF demagnetization of 5 - 10 mT and by thermal demagnetization in temperatures less than 300°C. The direction and magnetic characteristics (i.e., low coercivity and unblocking temperatures) of this component are consistent with an origin as a viscous remanent magnetization acquired in the present day field. Following removal of the secondary magnetization where present, the majority of diabase samples exhibited behavior characterized by the linear decay of the magnetic vector to the origin of a demagnetization diagram. The older 1270- 11 10 Ma limb of the loop is poorly constrained, while the depth of the loop, based on the 11 10- 1080 Ma Keweenawan data of the younger limb, is thoug

es failed to distinguish dykes of the northeast-trending Middle Proterozoic olivine-bearing Abitibi swarm from subparallel Early Proterozoic olivine-free Biscotasing (formerly Preissac) dykes, and hence paleomagnetic poles determined in these studies should no longer be used. In the present study, sampling of eight Abitibi dykes has identified 23 normally magnetized sites in four dykes and, for the first time, five reversely magnetized sites in three dykes. One of the normally magnetized sites corresponds to the locality for which a high-precision U-Pb age was previously reported. A baked contact test establishes that the characteristic remanence of one normally magnetized dyke is primary. In addition, sites along individual dykes exhibit much smaller secular variation than is observed between dykes, indicating that the remanences of the other dykes are also primary. One of the normally magnetized dykes, the 700 km long Great Abitibi dyke, exhibits two primary directions that correspond to two geochemically distinct magma pulses. The five normally magnetized units, which consist of four separate dykes plus the second pulse of the Great Abitibi dyke, yield a well- defined mean paleomagnetic pole at 42.8ON, 15 1 SOW, dm = 16.3", dp = 12.5". carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: 1, 1993 Paleomagnetic samples were collected from Mid-Pennsylvanian to Lower Permian red argillaceous cherts at two localities of the Slide Mountain terrane: 18 sites from the Sylvester allochthon in northern British Columbia and 11 sites from Sliding Mountain in central British Columbia. A secondary component of natural remanent magnetization in the Sylvester samples yields a paleomagnetic pole that can be brought into coincidence with the Jurassic portion of the North American apparent polar wander path by inferring vertical-axis rotation during obduction of the allochthon. Both localities yield a characteristic component (ChRM) with unblocking temperatures from 650 to 680°C. After structural correction for bedding tilt, all inclina- tions of ChRM are negative, consistent with magnetization during a reversed-polarity interval in the northern hemisphere. Site-mean ChRM directions show consistent inclinations but distinct stratigraphic groupings of declinations. Inclination-only statistics indicate that the ChRM passes a tilt test within the Sylvester allochthon and regionally between the two localities. The ChRM was apparently acquired prior to structural imbrication within the Sylvester section and regional differential tilting. We interpret the ChRM to be a primary magnetization acquired

Traces of drill barrel metal in some cases were found on the cores owing to the hardness of the cherts. Sample preparation included dipping all cores in a HCl bath to remove all traces of metal. In general, only one specimen was cut from each core. All paleomagnetic specimens were stored, measured, and demagnetized in a magnetically shielded room with field intensity < 200 nT. he origin of Uairen sediments is believed to be fluvial. They comprise conglomerates, sandstones, quartzites, quart- zose sandstones, and indurated sandstones. Intraformational conglomerates are common in the lowest part of the forma- tion: These are of economic importance, since diamonds and gold are found in streams that drain the conglomerates. Thin-section analyses of vertical and horizontal cuts of the Uairen sediments sampled for this study reveal a large amount (between 70 and 90 %) of quartz cemented by authigenic seri- cite and muscovite cemented by sericite. These samples are stained with iron hydroxide and they also show hematite, feld- spar, illite, zircon, microcline, apatite, epidote, and magne- tite. X-ray diffraction analyses revealed, in decreasing order of concentration, quartz, muscovite, feldspar, hematite, illite, magnetite, zircon, apatite, epidote, chlorite, tourmaline, pie- montite, and kaolinite. Previous paleomagnetic studies of these lava flows, known collectively as the Lake Shore Traps, have produced contradictory results. To investigate the cause of these conflicting results, 30 sites encompassing the most complete section of lava flows possible were collected and analyzed. Well-defined characteristic directions of magnetization were isolated using either alternating-field or thermal demagnetiza- tion or a combination of both. These directions of magnetization are interpreted as primary magnetizations acquired during the original cooling of the lavas. Hysteresis, thermomagnetic, and petrographic analyses suggest the carrier of magnetization is a pseudo-single-domain, titanium-poor magnetite that has undergone some high-temperature oxidation. Site means determined from the 30 lava flows define three distinct directional clusters. Each cluster of directions cor- responds to a different stratigraphic package of lava flows with the Copper Harbor Conglomerate. Between-site dispersion for each stratigraphic package or unit is much less than the expected value for Keweenawan-age rocks. Therefore, we suggest that most of the lava flows in each unit were extruded rapidly and that within an individual st

been adequately sampled. This explains why previous studies on the Lake Shore Traps have produced such different results; each study did not sample the entire range of directions possible in these lava flows. The paleomagnetic pole calculated from the 30 site-mean virtual geomagnetic poles is located at 22.2ON, 180.8"E (k = 35.0; A,, = 6.5"). The new Copper Harbor pole is now located in the appropriate chronological position with respect to the underlying Portage Lake Volcanics and the overlying Nonesuch Shale on the Keweenawan apparent polar wander path. The similarity of our Copper Harbor pole to that of the Portage Lake Volcanics reinforces the idea that the Copper Harbor Conglomerate is more closely related in time to the Portage Lake Volcanics than to the Nonesuch Shale. The unit is a reddish-brown, coarsely stratified pebble to boulder conglomerate with thin sandstone interbeds in its lower portion; higher in the section sandstone becomes the dominate facies. Conglomerate clasts are primarily rhyolitic, with approximately 10% being basal- tic. The thickness of the Copper Harbor Conglomerate ranges from 200 to 2000 m (White and Wright 1960; Daniels 1982), thickening toward the Lake Superior basin. White and Wright (1960) and more recently Elmore (1984) have interpreted the Copper Harbor Conglomerate as coalesced alluvial fans and sand flats deposited by northward-flowing streams originating from hills along the southern margin of the Lake Superior basin. The Copper Harbor Conglomerate interfingers with and conformably overlies the Portage Lake Volcanics, a 2500 - 5200 m series of subaerial flood basalts dated at approximately 1.1 Ga (White 1960; Van Schmus et al. 1982; Davis and Paces 1990). The Nonesuch Shale interfingers with and conformably overlies the Copper Harbor Conglomerate, which in turn is comformably overlain by the Freda Sandstone. Site means determined from the 30 lava flows define three distinct directional clusters. ch unit were extruded rapidly and that within an individual stratigraphic unit, paleosecular variation has not been adequately sampled. This explains why previous studies on the Lake Shore Traps have produced such different results; each study did not sample the entire range of directions possible in these lava flows. The paleomagnetic pole calculated from the 30 site-mean virtual geomagnetic poles is located at 22.2ON, 180.8"E (k = 35.0; A,, = 6.5"). The new Copper Harbor pole is now located in the appropriate chronological position with respect to the underlying Portage Lake Volcanics and the overlying Nonesuch Shale on the Keweenawan apparent polar wander path. The similarity of our Copper Harbor pole to that of the Portage Lake Volcanics reinforces the idea that the Copper Harbor Conglomerate is more closely related in time to the Portage Lake Volcanics than to the Nonesuch Shale. We have completed a paleomagnetic reconnaissance study of sedimentary and volcanic extrusive rocks collected from two major tectonic zones in northeastern Russia. Paleomagnetic sites were sampled within the fault-bounded structural units of the Khatyrka and Maynitsky superterranes and an overlap sequence of the Khatyrka superterrane. These sampling localities were chosen to allow both within-site and between-site fold tests. Stepwise thermal demagnetization within the temperature range ZOO-640°C showed a characteristic linear demagneti~tion path between thermal demagnetization steps of 400°C and SWC. For thermal steps above 55O”C, the magnetic intensity of many samples began to increase rapidly with magnetic directions, which were random between heating steps, suggesting the formation of new magnetic phases in these samples. Paleomagnetic samples collected from basalts and sediments of the Khatyrka superterrane and basalts and gabbros of the Maynitsky superterrane pass fold tests and show significant poleward motion of these superterranes since the formation of their rocks. The observed paleomagnetic paleolatitudes between 24”N or S and 32”N or S can be compared with expected paleolatitudes of 57”N to 79”N.

Because we are unsure as to whether individ- ual units making up the superterranes represent distinct terranes or complexly deformed portions PALEOMAGNETISM OF KHATYRKA AND MAYNITSKY SUPERTERRANES, RUSSIA 143 of a depositionally related unit, we shall refer to smaller zones as “structural units” of the larger superterranes. The Khatyrka superterrane consists of a series of fault-bounded structural units, which appear to have been sutured to this region of Eurasia dur- ing the upper Mesozoic (Ruzhentsev et al., 1982; Sokolov, 1988). The Ryelyavaamski structural unit occupies the lowest stratigraphic position in the paleomagnetic sampling region and is below the Ekonay, Kokuyskyi, and Iomraut structural units of the Khatyrka superterrane. An overlapping coarse elastic sequence of Senonian to Paleocene rocks locally covers these other structural units (Fig. 3). The Maynitsky superterrane is interpreted to represent a highly deformed, thrust-faulted, rem- nant of an island-arc complex. red gabbros, ul- trabasics, sheeted dikes and basalt flows. The most widely distributed formations in this structural unit are the tuffa- ceous sediments, which are characterized by relics of the Upper Jurassic to Valanginian radiolaria. The elastic component of these sediments con- sists of fragments of basalts, andesites, felsites, granitoids, schists, marbles, and mineral grains of quartz, plagioclase, biotite, epidote and apatite. Ash material constitutes l-50% of the rock vol- ume. Occasionally the sedimentary matrix con- sists of a poorly compacted clay-siliceous or clay-carbonate mass enriched with hematite. Ig- neous flows compose stratigraphic zones, which alternate with jaspers, red and black siliceous shales, pillow basalts and tuffs. Sampling localities 223 (sites 1 and 2) and 1412 (sites 1, 2, and 3) were taken from thin, tuff- terrigenous members of the Triassic portion of the Kokuyskyi structural unit of the Khatyrka superterrane. This unit is composed of blocks in a serpentinite matrix. Sheared serpentinites make up approximately half of the groundmass of this unit. The most widely distributed formations in this structural unit are the tuffa- ceous sediments, which are characterized by relics of the Upper Jurassic to Valanginian radiolaria. The elastic component of these sediments con- sists of fragments of basalts, andesites, felsites, granitoids, schists, marbles, and mineral grains of quartz, plagioclase, biotite, epidote and apatite. Ash material constitutes l-50% of the rock vol- ume. Occasionally the sedimentary matrix con- sists of a poorly compacted clay-siliceous or clay-carbonate mass enriched with hematite. Ig- neous flows compose stratigraphic zones, which alternate with jaspers, red and black siliceous shales, pillow basalts and tuffs. Sampling localities 223 (sites 1 and 2) and 1412 (sites 1, 2, and 3) were taken from thin, tuff- terrigenous members of the Triassic portion of the Kokuyskyi structural unit of the Khatyrka superterrane. This unit is composed of blocks in a serpentinite matrix. Sheared serpentinites make up approximately half of the groundmass of this unit. The elastic component of these sediments con- sists of fragments of basalts, andesites, felsites, granitoids, schists, marbles, and mineral grains of quartz, plagioclase, biotite, epidote and apatite. Ash material constitutes l-50% of the rock vol- ume. Occasionally the sedimentary matrix con- sists of a poorly compacted clay-siliceous or clay-carbonate mass enriched with hematite. Ig- neous flows compose stratigraphic zones, which alternate with jaspers, red and black siliceous shales, pillow basalts and tuffs. Sampling localities 223 (sites 1 and 2) and 1412 (sites 1, 2, and 3) were taken from thin, tuff- terrigenous members of the Triassic portion of the Kokuyskyi structural unit of the Khatyrka superterrane. Introduction Several previously published studies have ob- tained coherent characteristic magnetizations from the Late Permian Emeishan Basal& in southwest China (Table 1) in Sichuan, Guizhou and northern Yunnan provinces. Figure 1 (a,b) illustrates the sampling localities and the normal and reversed directions observed. It is clear that these directions are not antipodal and this has led to uncertainties about the validity of the Emeishan paleopoles. A comparison between Late Permian paleopoles from north and south China (e.g., Zhao and Coe, 1987) shows a large (ca. 70“) relative rotation of these two blocks. Similar Triassic declination differences suggest that the rotation occurred during the Jurassic at which time the two blocks were sutured together in the Qinling mobile belt. The details of the Permo-Triassic positions of the South China Block are obscure, however, because of the above-men- tioned uncertainties regarding the Emeishan poles. s B.V., Amsterdam 31 Palaeomagnetic results from the Permian Saint-Affrique basin (France) and implications for late and post-Hercynian tectonics A. Diego-Orozco a,b and B. Henry *Ya o Laborutoire de G&nagn&sme, ChXS and Unirlersite' Paris Vf, 4 aperrue de Neptune, 94107 Sa~t-~a~ Ceden, France ’ i~t~tuto Mexican0 del Petrbleo, Eje central L.&am C&denas 1.52, 07730 Mexico City, Mexico (Received July 2,1992; revised version accepted June 17, 1993) ABSTRACT Palaeomagnetic analyses have been carried out in sedimentary formations of the Permian Saint-Affrique basin of France and indicate a late Saxonian-early Thuringian age (the Dourdou sandstones) and at the top of the succession a middle Thuringian age (the Saint-Pierre pelites). Important rotations, clockwise. and anticlockwise, respectively, on the northern and southern borders of the basin, affected the Saint-Affrique area between the late Autunian and Saxonian. The opening of the basin occurred without rotation from the Saxonian to the middle Thuringian. Comparison with corresponding results from stable Europe, and in particular from the neighbouring Lodeve basin, indicates an anticlockwise rotation of the entire Saint-Affrique area of the order of 7” after the middle Thuringian (Palatine phase or a more recent tectonic ev

The magnetisations of the Lower Pliocene Trubi marls have maximum blocking temperatures indicating the presence of magnetite. In the simplest test, paleomagnetic declinations from coeval rocks 280 281 284’ a 0 around the arc are compared with each other or against a reference direction derived from a ref- erence apparent polar wander (APW) curve. If the declination differences are significant and of the correct sense, then a rotational origin for the arc is supposed. More rigorous tests utilize linear regression techniques, either by correlating bed- ding strike against declination (Schwartz and Van der Voo, 1983) or rotation (declination minus an appropriate reference declination) against the trend of the fold axes (Eldredge et al., 1985; Lowrie and Hirt, 1986). The orientation of folds around the Pennsylva- nia salient changes nearly 60” (Fig. 1). Fold axes on the northeastern limb of the salient trend nearly east-west while those on the southwestern limb of the salient trend north 30” east. Early paleomagnetic investigations in the region pro- duced contradictory results. Differences between the paleomagnetic declinations of the Upper Sil- urian Bloomsburg Formation (Irving and Opdyke, 1965; Roy et al., 1967) and Middle Silurian Rose Hill Formation (Graham, 1949) suggested at least partial oroclinal bending while the similarity of directions from the Lower Carbonifero

The difference in declination does not appear to be the result of internal deformation of the rocks or acquisition of magnetization during a period of rapid apparent polar wander. Rather, these directions indicate that the northeastern limb has been rotated clockwise 18 of: 9” relative to the southwestern limb. The sense and amount of this rotation is consistent with the curvature of the orogen around the salient. However, within each limb of the salient the primary component declinations do not directly correlate with the orientation of the first-order fold axes. (1985) also concluded that the salient was not a secondary feature. More recent paleomagnetic work has shown that many of the originally reported directions from these redbeds, especially from sites on the southwestern limb of the salient are contami- nated by secondary magnetizations (e.g. Kent and Opdyke, 1985). Using detailed thermal demagne- tization techniques, Kent and Opdyke (1985) were able to isolate two ancient magnetizations in the redbeds, a characteristic magnetization and a sec- ondary chemical remagnetization acquired during Alleghanian deformation in the Permian. In the simplest test, paleomagnetic declinations from coeval rocks 280 281 284’ a 0 around the arc are compared with each other or against a reference direction derived from a ref- erence apparent polar wander (APW) curve. If the declination differences are significant and of the correct sense, then a rotational origin for the arc is supposed. More rigorous tests utilize linear regression techniques, either by correlating bed- ding strike against declination (Schwartz and Van der Voo, 1983) or rotation (declination minus an appropriate reference declination) against the trend of the fold axes (Eldredge et al., 1985; Lowrie and Hirt, 1986). The new Andreas sites were collected on freshly exposed outcrops in the same road- works quarry sampled by Miller and Kent (1988a), and were used to augment their results. Samples were drilled either in the field using a portable drill fitted with a 2.5 cm diameter diamond coring bit or from hand samples using a similar-sized coring device. Samples were drilled either in the field using a portable drill fitted with a 2.5 cm diameter diamond coring bit or from hand samples using a similar-sized coring device. Samples were drilled either in the field using a portable drill fitted with a 2.5 cm diameter diamond coring bit or from hand samples using a similar-sized coring device. In the simplest test, paleomagnetic declinations from coeval rocks 280 281 284’ a 0 around the arc are compared with each other or against a reference direction derived from a ref- erence apparent polar wander (APW) curve. If the declination differences are significant and of the correct sense, then a rotational origin for the arc is supposed. More rigorous tests utilize linear regression techniques, either by correlating bed- ding strike against declination (Schwartz and Van der Voo, 1983) or rotation (declination minus an appropriate reference declination) against the trend of the fold axes (Eldredge et al., 1985; Lowrie and Hirt, 1986). In the simplest test, paleomagnetic declinations from coeval rocks 280 281 284’ a 0 around the arc are compared with each other or against a reference direction derived from a ref- erence apparent polar wander (APW) curve. If the declination differences are significant and of the correct sense, then a rotational origin for the arc is supposed. More rigorous tests utilize linear regression techniques, either by correlating bed- ding strike against declination (Schwartz and Van der Voo, 1983) or rotation (declination minus an appropriate reference declination) against the trend of the fold axes (Eldredge et al., 1985; Lowrie and Hirt, 1986). The orientation of folds around the Pennsylva- nia salient changes nearly 60” (Fig. 1). Fold axes on the northeastern limb of the salient trend nearly east-west while those on the southwestern limb of the salient trend north 30” east. Samples were drilled either in the field using a portable drill fitted with a 2.5 cm diameter diamond coring bit or from hand samples using a similar-sized coring device. The new Andreas sites were collected on freshly exposed outcrops in the same road- works quarry sampled by Miller and Kent (1988a), and were used to augment their results. Samples were drilled either in the field using a portable drill fitted with a 2.5 cm diameter diamond coring bit or from hand samples using a similar-sized coring device. Samples were oriented using a standard paleomagnetic orientation device and magnetic compass. Bedding orientations were measured in the field with a Brunton compass. The magnetization of these rocks is too weak to deflect the compass readings. Progressive thermal demagnetization (8-15 steps) was performed on all samples using a Schonstedt TSD-1 thermal demagnetizer. Rema- nence measurements were made on a three-axis cryogenic magnetometer. Magnetic components were determined by fitting a least square regres- sion line to the linear portions of the demagneti- zation trajectories. The distribution of sample directions was calculated using Fisher statistics (Fisher, 1953). Incremental fold tests were per- formed using 5% increments of limb dip unfolded about the line of strike. Although the exact nature of the remagnetization process is not yet known, growth of new magnetic phases as the rocks interacted with chemically active brines during the Alleghanian orogeny is considered the most probable remagnetization mechanism (Oliver, 1986). Discussion This study reinforces the identification by ear- lier studies of a ubiquitous overprinting ChRM temporally linked to Variscan Orogenesis. A comparable magnetisation associated with com- pressional tectonics is also common along the foreland of the North American extension of this orogen. At the Appalachian margin it is at- tributed to growth of authigenic hematite medi- ated by fluid migration motivated by nappe stack- ing and lithospheric thickening (Oliver, 1986; Mc- Cabe and Elmore, 1989). In South Wales, rema- nence acquisition is contemporary with develop- ment of an Upper Carboniferous foreland basin (Setiabudidaya et al., 1994) and fluids responsible for chemical remagnetisation appear to have mi- grated up dip in sandstone aquifers of the Old Red Sandstone (Channel1 et al., 1992). Discussion This study reinforces the identification by ear- lier studies of a ubiquitous overprinting ChRM temporally linked to Variscan Orogenesis. A comparable magnetisation associated with com- pressional tectonics is also common along the foreland of the North American extension of this orogen. At the Appalachian margin it is at- tributed to growth of authigenic hematite medi- ated by fluid migration motivated by nappe stack- ing and lithospheric thickening (Oliver, 1986; Mc- Cabe and Elmore, 1989). Introduction The palaeoma~etic properties of Lower Palaeozoic rocks from Africa, and hence Gond- wanaland, remain very poorly defined and con- troversial. carrier_identity_candidates.excerpt: mber 1993) Abstract To contribute to the understanding of the Cenozoic tectonic history of China, and eastern Eurasia in general, we collected paleomagnetic samples from Tertiary rocks in both North and South China. Our Miocene paleomagnetic data for northern China are from four widely separated basalt sections in the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region and Shandong Province. Both normal and reversed polarities of the characteristic magnetization are present in the stratigraphic sequence, and the mean normal and reversed directions are closely antiparallel to each other. The fact that the same characteristic direction was carried by both magnetite and hematite suggests that the hematite was probably formed by auto-oxidation processes during primary cooling of the basalts. The paleomagnetic data from these four areas also pass a regional generalized fold test. The corresponding mean Miocene paleomagnetic pole for northern China is longitude 261.6”E, latitude 88.3”N (A,, = 6.4”). Our Early Tertiary paleomagnetic results for south China are from two sandstone sections around the city of Nanning (22.7”N, 108.3”E3 in Guangxi Zhuang Au- tonomous Region. High-temperature characteristic directions isolated in 31 samples from five sites pass both tilt and reversal tests. The paleomagneti

ity (Hongshiya) were typically of the order of 1 A/M. Thermal, aIternating field (AF), and com- bined (thermal after AF) demagnetizations were conducted, in an attempt to remove possible isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) caused by lightning strikes. After removal of a low-un- blocking temperature component between 100” and 3OO”C, the samples yielded a well-defined characteristic magnetization, as shown by demag- netization plots that almost all reached a stable end point (Fig. 3a). Combined demagnetization and isothermal remanent acquisition experiments suggest that the characteristic magnetization is probably carried by magnetite. Both normal and reversed polarities of the characteristic direction are present in the stratigraphic sequence. In ad- dition, an intermediate direction is observed in samples from the middle portion of the same stratigraphic section. These samples are overlain by lavas of reversed polarity and underlain by lavas of normal polarity, suggesting that lava flows at this locality span a polarity transition. The Plio-Pleistocene nonmarine Saugus Formation is widely exposed in the east Ventura basin and the northern San Fernando Valley, north and south of the Santa Susana fault. In the east Ventura basin, the Saugus is overlain by the Pacoima Formation. Magnetostratigraphy of the fine- grained Saugus and Pacoima strata and the presence of the 0.76 Ma Bishop ash are used to calculate their average sedi- mentation rates: 0.9 km/m.y. in the east Ventura basin and 1.1 km/m.y. in the northern San Fernando Valley. Extrapo- lation of the Saugus and Pacoima sedimentation rates shows that they were deposited from about 2.3 to 0.5 Ma both north and south of the Santa Susana fault. The shift from remote to locally derived clasts marks the initiation of uplift of the Santa Susana Mountains. The extrapolated age of this boundary is about 0.7-0.6 Ma. INTRODUCTION The Santa Susana fault is part of a discontinuous reverse- fault system, north side up, extending east from Santa Barbara to the San Jacinto fault near San Bernardino (Figure 1). Other faults in this system include the Red Mountain, San Cayetano, San Fernando, Sierra Madre, and Cucamonga faults. The fault dies out to the northwest near the Santa Clara Valley, where strata of Miocene and Pliocene age are contin- uous across the westward projection of the fault [Yeats, 1987]. The fault contains two left-stepping lateral ramps, one at Gillibrand Canyon (GC, Figure 2) in the central part of the fault, and one farther east at the northwest edge of the San Fernando Valley (SF, Figure 2). East of the San Fernando lateral ramp, the fault breaks up into several strands, at least one of which moved during the 1971 San Fernando earthquake. The Modelo Formation (middle-late Miocene), Towsley Formation (latest Miocene-earliest Pliocene), and Fernando Formation (Pliocene) were influenced by the old depositional hinge line, northeast side down, and thus they predate the Santa Susana fault. The Torrey and Frew reverse faults cut the Fernando Formation and are overlain unconformably by the Quaternary Saugus Formation [Yeats, 1979, 1987]. Absence of scarp-derived detritus from these pre-Saugus faults suggests that they were not accompanied by extensive subaerial uplift of their hanging walls. gon State University, Corvallis Abstract. The Plio-Pleistocene nonmarine Saugus Formation is widely exposed in the east Ventura basin and the northern San Fernando Valley, north and south of the Santa Susana fault. In the east Ventura basin, the Saugus is overlain by the Pacoima Formation. Magnetostratigraphy of the fine- grained Saugus and Pacoima strata and the presence of the 0.76 Ma Bishop ash are used to calculate their average sedi- mentation rates: 0.9 km/m.y. in the east Ventura basin and 1.1 km/m.y. in the northern San Fernando Valley. Extrapo- lation of the Saugus and Pacoima sedimentation rates shows that they were deposited from about 2.3 to 0.5 Ma both north and south of the Santa Susana fault. The shift from remote to locally derived clasts marks the initiation of uplift of the Santa Susana Mountains. The extrapolated age of this boundary is about 0.7-0.6 Ma. INTRODUCTION The Santa Susana fault is part of a discontinuous reverse- fault system, north side up, extending east from Santa Barbara to the San Jacinto fault near San Bernardino (Figure 1). Other faults in this system include the Red Mountain, San Cayetano, San Fernando, Sierra Madre, and Cucamonga faults. The 1971 San Fernando earthquake (M = 6.4) and smaller earth- quakes on the Red Moun

ists, 1992; here- inafter referred to as Yeats et al., submitted manuscrit, 1992). The fault dies out to the northwest near the Santa Clara Valley, where strata of Miocene and Pliocene age are contin- uous across the westward projection of the fault [Yeats, 1987]. The fault contains two left-stepping lateral ramps, one at Gillibrand Canyon (GC, Figure 2) in the central part of the fault, and one farther east at the northwest edge of the San Fernando Valley (SF, Figure 2). East of the San Fernando lateral ramp, the fault breaks up into several strands, at least one of which moved during the 1971 San Fernando earthquake. The Modelo Formation (middle-late Miocene), Towsley Formation (latest Miocene-earliest Pliocene), and Fernando Formation (Pliocene) were influenced by the old depositional hinge line, northeast side down, and thus they predate the Santa Susana fault. The Torrey and Frew reverse faults cut the Fernando Formation and are overlain unconformably by the Quaternary Saugus Formation [Yeats, 1979, 1987]. Absence of scarp-derived detritus from these pre-Saugus faults suggests that they were not accompanied by extensive subaerial uplift of their hanging walls. The Saugus Formation [Kew, 1924; Winterer and Durham, 1962], the main subject of this magnetostratigraphic study, occupies the center of the east Ventura basin where it is conformable with underlying Pliocene strata. South of the Santa Susana fault, the Saugus occurs in discontinuous patches that unconformably overlie faulted strata as old as Eocene that are overridden by the Santa Susana fault [Yeats, 1987]. The Cuyama basin in the southern Coast Ranges of California underwent a transition from strike-slip to compres- sional faulting, synchronous with the deposition of the Pliocene-Pleistocene Morales Formation. Paleomagnetic stratigraphy was used to date the Morales Formation and, by inference, the beginning of compressional tectonics. Sections sampled below the Whiterock and Morales thrusts in the western Cuyama basin are predominantly normal and are correlated with the Gauss chron (3.57-2.60 Ma). An abrupt appearance of clasts derived from the overlying thrust sheet in the section below the Whiterock thrust suggests uplift of the Caliente Range during the middle to late Gauss chron. Seismic reflection data indicate that the eastern sections were deposited earlier. In conjunction with fossil evidence, the eastern sections are correlated to a time between the late Gilbert and early Matuyama chrons. The presence of a crys- talline boulder bed midway in an eastern Cuyama basin section indicates uplift of the Mount Pinos-Frazier Mountain highlands during the Matuyama chron between 2.60 and 0.78 Ma. Paleomagnetic directions of the Morales Formation document approximately 23 ø clockwise rotation of the Cuyama basin. INTRODUCTION The Cuyama basin, located northwest of the western Big Bend of the San Andreas Fault (Figures 1 and 2), is an area of transition from strike-slip tectonics of the Coast Ranges to the northwest and compressional tectonics of the Transverse Ranges to the south. The Cuyama basin is part of the Salinian block, which is bounded by right-lateral strike-slip faults. It is north of the Big Pine fault, the northern boundary of the compressional Transverse Ranges. In the Cuyama basin, the change in tectonic styles from strike-slip to compression in- volves the Pliocene-Pleistocene fluvial Morales Formation. During the Pleistocene, structural deformation of the Cuyama Valley changed from strike-slip faulting to predomi- nantly folding and thrust faulting. The Russell strike-slip fault, known only from the subsurface of the Cuyama Valley, may be an older, inactive strand of the San Andreas fault [Yeats et al., 1989]. Such comparisons can yield precise estimates of rotations because they circumvent uncertainties produced by directional dispersion due to paleosecular variation. Without independent information, however, it is not possible to deter- mine which sites actually rotated with respect to the stable cra- ton. Moreover, such rotation estimates may be strongly affected by any site-specific errors such as unit misidentification or inac- curate tilt correction. An alternative method to assess rotation is to calculate a mean remanence direction from a number of tem- porally discrete volcanic units from a locality to average the paleosecular variation. This time-averaged direction is then compared to an expected direction calculated from an appropri- ate cratonic paleopole. Rotation estimates of this type com- monly are not as precise as relative rotations determined from individual units unless they incorporate data from a large num- ber of volcanic units because they must average paleosecular variation. Rotations based on time-averaged directions, how- ever, have the advantage of being \"absolute\" in sense and magnitude relative to the craton and of being less affected by random site-speci

cases [Hudson, 1992]. For silicic lavas, only sites from flow interiors were used to avoid any dispersion related to post- blocking rotation of flow margins. Stratal attitudes of ash flow tuff sites were estimated by measurements of compaction folia- tions, stratigraphic contacts, and boundaries between welding zones, or were estimated from three-point calculations of exten- sive stratigraphic contacts. Attitudes for lava flows were derived from three-point calculations for extensive exposures or were extrapolated from nearby ashflow tuffs of similar age. In the laboratory, samples were subjected to progressive alternating field or thermal demagnetization. At least six sam- ples from each site were subjected to alternating field (AF) demagnetization (typically eight demagnetization steps per sample to peak inductions of 80 millitesla (mT)). No clockwise vertical-axis rotation is found to support projection of dextral faults of the Walker Lane beneath the central SWNVF. Clockwise rotation of variable magnitude is common at numerous sites from southern and western margins of the field. ll locality mean declinations were found to be deflected westward with respect to the Eurasian paleomeridian. The proposed counter-clockwise rotation of the Fergana block during the late Cenozoic is shown to account for the main features of the Alpine tectonics. In particular, the 200 km offset along the Talas-Fergana fault is connected with rotation, which contradicts the common idea that this displacement is of Late Paleozoic age. The horizontal movements are most probably not older than 10 Ma. Introduction The Tien Shan tectonic realm is an example of an ancient mobile zone re-activated by younger tectonics. After Late Paleozoic deformation, al- most no tectonic activity took place here during the Mesozoic and Paleogene. In the Neogene, both the Caledonian and Variscan belts were gradually remobilized and the most intense defor- mation was in the Pliocene-Quaternary. This ac- tivity is usually linked with the India-Eurasia collision (Molnar and Tapponnier, 1975). How- ever, the relative intensity of the Variscan and Alpine tectonics is not clear. The prevailing opin- ion is that the Alpine movements inherited the older structural pattern and slightly reworked it. In contrast, other geologists think that the mod- ern structural pattern is mainly Late Cenozoic and a

nherited the older structural pattern and slightly reworked it. In contrast, other geologists think that the mod- ern structural pattern is mainly Late Cenozoic and a result of Alpine movements (e.g., Yablon- skaya, 1989). Paleomagnetism may solve this problem, but the results reported so far are not conclusive. Data on the Cretaceous from various authors (Khramov, 1984), are contradictory, in terms of both sign and magnitude of rotation. The main body of the results is based on natural remanent magnetization (NRM) data or NRM after limited cleaning and does not satisfy modem reliability criteria. A result from Lower Cretaceous basalts from the north of the Fergana Basin (Eroshkin, 1991) was obtained after complete stepwise de- magnetization and confirmed with the reversal test. However, its value is limited because only three lava flows were studied. Some data on Pliocene sediments from the Fergana Basin (Khaydarov, 1987) were interpreted as showing about 10” of counter-clockwise rotation. This ex- planation is not unique, however, since the decli- nation anomaly might stem from primary tilts of sedimentary rocks which have accumulated in 0040-1951/93/$06.00 0 1993 - Elsevier Science Publishers B.V. ll locality mean declinations were found to be deflected westward with respect to the Eurasian paleomeridian. The proposed counter-clockwise rotation of the Fergana block during the late Cenozoic is shown to account for the main features of the Alpine tectonics. In particular, the 200 km offset along the Talas-Fergana fault is connected with rotation, which contradicts the common idea that this displacement is of Late Paleozoic age. The horizontal movements are most probably not older than 10 Ma. Introduction The Tien Shan tectonic realm is an example of an ancient mobile zone re-activated by younger tectonics. After Late Paleozoic deformation, al- most no tectonic activity took place here during the Mesozoic and Paleogene. In the Neogene, both the Caledonian and Variscan belts were gradually remobilized and the most intense defor- mation was in the Pliocene-Quaternary. This ac- tivity is usually linked with the India-Eurasia collision (Molnar and Tapponnier, 1975). How- ever, the relative intensity of the Variscan and Alpine tectonics is not clear. The prevailing opin- ion is that the Alpine movements inherited the older structural pattern and slightly reworked it. In contrast, other geologists think that the mod- ern structural pattern is mainly Late Cenozoic and a

nherited the older structural pattern and slightly reworked it. In contrast, other geologists think that the mod- ern structural pattern is mainly Late Cenozoic and a result of Alpine movements (e.g., Yablon- skaya, 1989). Paleomagnetism may solve this problem, but the results reported so far are not conclusive. Data on the Cretaceous from various authors (Khramov, 1984), are contradictory, in terms of both sign and magnitude of rotation. The main body of the results is based on natural remanent magnetization (NRM) data or NRM after limited cleaning and does not satisfy modem reliability criteria. A result from Lower Cretaceous basalts from the north of the Fergana Basin (Eroshkin, 1991) was obtained after complete stepwise de- magnetization and confirmed with the reversal test. However, its value is limited because only three lava flows were studied. Some data on Pliocene sediments from the Fergana Basin (Khaydarov, 1987) were interpreted as showing about 10” of counter-clockwise rotation. This ex- planation is not unique, however, since the decli- nation anomaly might stem from primary tilts of sedimentary rocks which have accumulated in 0040-1951/93/$06.00 0 1993 - Elsevier Science Publishers B.V. A low-temperature (LT) component is removed between 100 and 300-320°C and it is carried by iron sulphides; a high-temperature (HT) component is removed between 300-320 and 430-450°C and is probably carried by titano- magnetites. Introduction For two main reasons the Paleozoic rocks of the Ardenno-Rhenish Massif and the Brabant Massif (Fig. 1) have to a large extent not seen any paleomagnetic research: firstly, the intense rock deformation impedes the reconstruction of pre- tectonic magnetic directions and no general method exists to correct internal rock deforma- tion (Lowrie et al., 1986; CognC and Perroud, 1987); secondly, in most cases primary magnetiza- tions often have been completely overprinted by the Variscan remagnetization (McCabe and El- more, 1989). Paleomagnetic data are of special significance for the reconstruction of Variscan Central Eu- rope. Geotectonic models of the Variscides may be placed into two groups, those based predomi- nantly on paleomagnetic data and those based partly on such data. In the first group are those developed by Perroud e

t-Namur Synclino- rium and Inde Syncline (Fig. 1). The massifs of Brabant, Stavelot-Venn and Rocroi consist of Cambrian-Silurian elastic sedi- ments of the early Paleozoic Ardennes Basin, which have been folded in the Caledonian orogeny under low-grade metamorphic conditions (Walter, 1980). During the Devonian and Early Carbonif- erous, the development of the Variscan geosyn- cline resulted in the deposition of more than 6000 m of sediments in the Dinant-Namur Synclino- rium and more than 4000 m in the Inde Syncline. In the Asturian phase the sediments of the Sub- variscan marginal basin were folded and faulted. This Variscan deformation resulted in E-W- to NE-SW-trending foid structures. Junggar, along with northern Tianshan, therefore represents the part of the late Paleozoic continental margin of the already amalgamated Siberia and Kazakhstan blocks. Collision along Tianshan between Tarim and Junggar has been inferred to be in the Early Permian based on geological features such as termination of andesitic volcanism, the development of unconformities between late Early Permian and underlying units [Xinjiang Stratigraphic Group, 1981], the intrusion of widespread syncollisional to postcollisional granites in Tianshan [Xinjiang Bureau of Geology and Mineral Resources, 1985; Coleman, 1989], and mixture of Angaran and Cathaysian flora across Tianshan [Wu, 1983; Hu, 1985]. This interpretation has recently been challenged by McFadden et al. [1988], who proposed that there was still a wide ocean between Tarim and Kazakhstan in the Late Permian to Early Triassic, based on a comparison of paleomagnetic results. We summarize our paleomagnetic study in Tianshan that provides new constraint on both the timing of collision between Tarim and Eurasia and also the paleolatitudinal position of northern Tianshan/southem Junggar. [1988], who proposed that there was still a wide ocean between Tarim and Kazakhstan in the Late Permian to Early Triassic, based on a comparison of paleomagnetic results. One specimen per site was chosen to perform a pilot-trial study to analyze the general demagnetization behavior of the samples. During the pilot-trial, the samples were heated at intervals of 50øC below 350øC, and 20øC or 30øC above 350øC, commonly including 12 or more steps. This provided good control on the critical transitional points for demagnetization curves so that fewer steps (usually 8-10) were necessary for thermally demagnetizing the remaining samples. section_candidates.excerpt: ISM OF LATE PALEOZOIC ROCKS IN THE TIANSHAN, NORTHWESTERN CHINA Nie Shangyou and David B. Rowley Department of Geophysical Sciences, University of Chicago, Chicago, Illinois Rob Van der Voo Department of Geological Sciences, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan Li Maosong Department of Geological Sciences, Beijing University, Beijing, China Abstract. A paleomagnetic study of late Paleozoic rocks in two areas of northwestern China helps to constrain the timing of collision between Tarim and the Junggar part of Eurasia along Tianshan. A primary Late Permian direction (D/I = 198/- 59, K=24, A95=12.6) is derived from seven sites (53 samples) from the Heavenly Lake (Tianzhi) section in northern Tianshan that has both normal and reversed polarities and passes a fold test at the 99% confidence level. This result gives a latitude of 39øN in the Late Permian for southern Junggar. Twenty-two sites (144 samples) from the Devonian and Carboniferous rocks across Tianshan reveal postfolding remagnetizations some of which are interpreted as being acquired in the Permian due to the Tarim-Eurasia collision. The Late Permian paleomagnetic pole from the Heavenly Lake section is statistically indistinguishable from three published Late Permian poles from Tarim indicatin

turing of Tarim and Junggar before that time. These paleomagnetic poles from northwestern China are, however, significantly different from those of stable Eurasia, suggesting substantial later relative motion that can be partly accounted for by the progressive closure of the Mongolo- Okhotsk ocean and associated tectonic rotations. The absence of a discernable Permian ocean record west of the Khangay highland in central Mongolia requires that the rotations be accommodated within a diffusive plate boundary in the Eurasian continent. A Late Permian continental plate reconstruction is presented that takes into consideration these new paleomagnetic results and other geological constraints. INTRODUCTION China comprises at least 11 different continental fragments and arc-related assemblages, including three major continental blocks of South China (equivalent to Yangtze), North China (equivalent to Sino-Korean), and Tarim, and eight smaller continental and arc-related fragments, with Junggar in the northwest, Dahinggan and Xingkai-Bureya in the northeast, and Qaidam (QD), Central Kunlun (CKL), Eastern Qiangtang (EQ), Western Qiangtang (WQ), and Lhasa in the southwest (Figure 1). Biogeographically, Junggar, Dahinggan, and Xingkai-Bureya in the north are closely related to the Siberia

in to the south, and within it are the Turpan basin in the east and Yining basin in the west (Figure 2). The NW-SE trending Irtysh-Bayatik (IT-BY) suture separates Siberia from Kazakhstan prior to its Late Carboniferous closure (Figure 1) [Rowley et al., 1985; Zonenshain et al., 1990] and clearly extends into China through northwestern Junggar. This boundary extends southeastward from the ophiolitic melanges north of Karamay to the Kelameili ophiolites within the southern Altay in northeastern Junggar. This southeast trend is almost perpendicular to the present structural trend of northwestern Junggar, which reflects more recent deformation. Most of Junggar between this Irtysh-Bayatik and Kelameili line in the north and northern Tianshan in the south was apparently the eastern extension of Kazakhstan. Junggar, along with northern Tianshan, therefore represents the part of the late Paleozoic continental margin of the already amalgamated Siberia and Kazakhstan blocks. Collision along Tianshan between Tarim and Junggar has been inferred to be in the Early Permian based on geological features such as termination of andesitic volcanism, the development of unconformities between late Early Permian and underlying units [Xinjiang Stratigraphic Group, 1981], the intrusion of

and Kelameili line in the north and northern Tianshan in the south was apparently the eastern extension of Kazakhstan. Junggar, along with northern Tianshan, therefore represents the part of the late Paleozoic continental margin of the already amalgamated Siberia and Kazakhstan blocks. Collision along Tianshan between Tarim and Junggar has been inferred to be in the Early Permian based on geological features such as termination of andesitic volcanism, the development of unconformities between late Early Permian and underlying units [Xinjiang Stratigraphic Group, 1981], the intrusion of widespread syncollisional to postcollisional granites in Tianshan [Xinjiang Bureau of Geology and Mineral Resources, 1985; Coleman, 1989], and mixture of Angaran and Cathaysian flora across Tianshan [Wu, 1983; Hu, 1985]. This interpretation has recently been challenged by McFadden et al. [1988], who proposed that there was still a wide ocean between Tarim and Kazakhstan in the Late Permian to Early Triassic, based on a comparison of paleomagnetic results. We summarize our paleomagnetic study in Tianshan that provides new constraint on both the timing of collision between Tarim and Eurasia and also the paleolatitudinal position of northern Tianshan/southem Junggar. Several recent analyses of North American paleomagnefic data suggest fast apparent polar wander (APW) (--0.75ø/m.y.) during the Late Triassic and a modest amount (-5 ø) of Colorado Plateau clockwise rotation. Paleomagnetic poles from the lower (Carnian), middle (NorJan), and upper (Hettangian) stratigraphic intervals of the Newark Basin, however, indicate very slow APW over the Late Triassic and provide an alternative interpretation for plateau rotation. The middle Newark pole is supported by positive fold and reversal tests, precluding remagnetization, and agrees well with the pole reported from the Norian Upper Shale Member of the Chinle Formation from east central New Mexico as well as the 214 Ma Manicouagan pole from Quebec. These poles provide a well- defined mean NorJan reference pole for eratonic North America at 57.4øN 91.0øE A95=3.8 ø. Paleomagnetic poles from the Chinle Formation on the Colorado Plateau (Owl Rock Member, Church Rock Member, and our new result from the upper Chinle in Utah) are also well grouped, consistent with slow APW over the NorJan, but give a mean pole position (57.7øN 65.6øE A95=2.5 ø) that differs significantly from the Norian pole for eratonic North America. einer [1988] suggested that the Colorado Plateau experienced a separate rotation in the Late Permian, prior to the Laramide and Cenozoic rotations that are of interest here. The tectonic implication of the Permian poles is complicated, however, by new evidence that portions of central New Mexico east of the Rio Grande Rift, where some key Permian poles that have been regarded as cratonic references were obtained, experienced a similar sense of rotation as the Colorado Plateau [Molina-Garza et al., 1991]. Our attention therefore focuses on the Triassic for which recent paleomagnetic studies provide what we regard as more coherent information to separate North American APW from Colorado Plateau rotation. Our synthesis supports the virtual absence of APW in the Late Triassic that was independently suggested by the Newark results and shows that post-Triassic net clockwise rotation of the Colorado Plateau must have been consequently large. The declination of 13 ° is rotated 7 ° clockwise, in contrast to Paleogene and Late Mesozoic directions from the Marche-Umbria region of central Italy, which usually show anti- clockwise rotations [18]. The A- and C-component directions are dis- persed along a great circle that passes through the B-, D- and ChRM mean directions and the present ADF direction. Many of the A-compo- nent directions are close to the ADF direction; the remainder, together with the C-component directions, are streaked along this great circle between the ADF direction and the reverse ChRM direction (Figs. 7a and c). We conclude that the A- and C-components are normal over- prints, primarily due to partial remagnetization in a recent field, and contaminated by an unre- moved element of the B-component. The A-com- ponent is probably a simple viscous overprint. The C-component is defined in a range of un- blocking temperatures above the Curie point of maghemite. It was not possible to identify the magnetic mineral carrying this component defini- tively. Its blocking temperature spectrum was narrow, suggesting it may be carried by a limited range of grain sizes. The predominance of mag- netite in these rocks suggests that it might be a secondary phase of magnetite. Examples have been reported where secondary magnetite formed in carbonate rocks from iron-rich fluids that were able to permeate the rocks during tectonic defor- mation [19-21]. As there are no flow or 'cooling units' that can be uniquely correlated across the fault, the rotation and flattening statistics are given with respect to the Miocene reference field rather than between the two areas. The results indicate that significant differential rotation has occurred between the Pink Canyon and Central Mesa ar- eas. The angular dispersion of the site-mean direc- tions, the presence of a reversed-polarity site, and the age range of the volcanic sequence suggest that the secular variation of the geomagnetic field has been at least partially averaged in this study. section_candidates.excerpt: d 27 June 1994 Abstract Paleomagnetic data, coupled with detailed geological analysis of the southeastern Goldstone Lake region, indicate that lower Miocene volcanic and epiclastic rocks of the Pink Canyon area have been folded, faulted and tectonically rotated ~ 28.4 _+ 9.0 ° clockwise about a vertical axis; identical rocks lying to the west across the Goldstone Lake Fault (east branch) have been rotated 9.6 _+ 7.4 °. The Coyote Canyon Fault is locally folded about a vertical axis ~ 25 ° in a clockwise sense in the Pink Canyon area. Timing relationships indicate that rotation is post-early Miocene; regional relationships imply that deformation is late Miocene to Holocene in age. These relationships imply that tectonic rotation is local rather than regional in extent as proposed by some tectonic models. The results of this study are generally consistent with the Dokka and Travis [1] model and the subsequently revised Dokka model [2] of strain partitioning in the northeastern Mojave Desert block. 1. Paleomagnetic data are presented for Late Creta- ceous volcanic and intrusive rocks in the Tombstone district and Dos Cabezas Mountains of southeastern Arizona. The resultant paleopole (73øN, 224øE, A95= 8 ø) is similar to a Late Cretaceous reference pole for North America (82øN, 210øE, A95 = 7ø), implying that these rocks have not been significantly rotated about vertical or near-vertical axes relative to the continental interior. Generally, concordant results have also been published for Pennsylvanian terra rosa paleosols within the Black Prince Limestone at localities in the nearby Gunnison Hills, Whetstone Mountains, and Naco Hills. Together, however, these Carboniferous data indicate a 9 ø + 7 ø clockwise rotation, with respect to North America, similar to that determined for the Colorado Plateau (5ø-14 ø ) since the mid-Cretaceous. Published paleomagnetic data for rocks south and west of the Tombstone vicinity indicate much larger clockwise rotations ranging from -25 ø to -60 ø , im- plying that a rotational domain boundary runs between the Mustang Mountains and Canelo Hills to the southeast and between the Silver Bell and Tucson Mountains to the northwest. ceous reference palcopoles for the North American plate, implying that these rocks are also unrotated. Combining the new data with those available for other localities in southeastern Arizona, we propose a simple pattern of rotated and unrotated domains in the region separated by a northwest trending boundary. Geologic Setting During Mesozoic time, southeastern Arizona was part of a continental margin volcanic arc that extended along the North American Cordillera from Mexico to Alaska. Jurassic and Cretaceous silicic volcanic rocks are well preserved and only weakly metamorphosed in the region, but they have been structurally dismembered and fragmented due to repeated deformation that includes Laramide compression, middle Tertiary extension, and late Cenozoic block faulting. In south- ern Arizona the Laramide orogeny has been divided into three phases [e.g., Miller et al., 1992], an initial phase characterized by compressional basement-cored block uplift; a medial phase of major plutonism, porphyry copper mineralization, and regional uplift; and a waning phase of compressional tectonics, plutonism, and volcanism. Northwest trending faults with probable strike-slip displacement are a major tectonic element of southeastern Arizona [Titley, 1976; Drewes, 1981], and Keith and Wilt [1986] have associated left-lateral movement on these faults with the roedial phase (65 to 55 Ma) of Laramide deformation. Remanent magnetization was measured with either a cryogenic magnetometer (LETI) or a Schonstedt spinner flux gate magnetometer. We isolated characteristic directions of remanent magnetism after progressive thermal demagnetization or alternating field demagnetization, performed with Schonstedt equipment. In general, we found thermal cleaning to be more efficient for sediments. At each step in the demagnetization process, we measured bulk susceptibility. We determined paleomagnetic directions by principal component analysis, within a graphical interactive system [Perroud, 1985], and we used the statistics of Fisher [1953]. We studied one specimen from each core and two specimens from each hand sample. We considered as reliable any site which presented consistent magnetic behavior from at least three samples. Fold tests were carried out in two ways, according to McElhinny [1964] and McFadden and Jones [1981]. For some localities, the number of sites which yielded acceptable results was rather limited and so we had to use sample directions. The algorithm, on which is based the test of McFadden and Jones [1981], was used in three different ways. First, we compared mean directions from different localities within a single basin, to see if the differences were statistically significant (the consistency test). To further explore the magnetic mineralogy of our rocks, we conducted an additional experiment on seven samples, from sites IC, IR, IS, IY, IZ, I2 and I5, following a method suggested by Lowrie [1990], in which different coercivity fractions of IRM are magnetized in successively smaller fields, along three orthogonal directions, and then thermally demagnetized. The three-component IRMs were produced in fields of, first, 1.2 T along the Z axis; then, 0.15 T along the X axis; and finally, 0.05 T along the Y axis. These fields were chosen so as to evaluate the influence of hematite and goethite for the Z axis, single-domain magnetite for the X axis and low- coercivity magnetite for the Yaxis. Remanent magnetization was measured with either a cryogenic magnetometer (LETI) or a Schonstedt spinner flux gate magnetometer. We isolated characteristic directions of remanent magnetism after progressive thermal demagnetization or alternating field demagnetization, performed with Schonstedt equipment. In general, we found thermal cleaning to be more efficient for sediments. At each step in the demagnetization process, we measured bulk susceptibility. We determined paleomagnetic directions by principal component analysis, within a graphical interactive system [Perroud, 1985], and we used the statistics of Fisher [1953]. We studied one specimen from each core and two specimens from each hand sample. We considered as reliable any site which presented consistent magnetic behavior from at least three samples. Fold tests were carried out in two ways, according to McElhinny [1964] and McFadden and Jones [1981]. For some localities, the number of sites which yielded acceptable results was rather limited and so we had to use sample directions. The algorithm, on which is based the test of McFadden and Jones [1981], was used in three different ways. First, we compared mean directions from different localities within a single basin, to see if the differences were statistically significant (the consistency test). The Dzhety-Ogyuz Formation consists of red sandstones and conglomerates. Remnants of an Oligocene tortoise have been found at the type locality of Dzhety-Ogyuz [Sidorenko, 1972]. The formation is here more than 1000 m thick and the top may be Lower Miocene. The bedding dips gently to the NNW. We sampled 12 sites, seven near the base of the formation (IT to IZ) and five near the top (I1 to I5). Seven randomly oriented pebbles were sampled at one of the sites, in order to perform a conglomerate test. At the Karakoo locality, on the southwestern edge of the Issyk-Kul basin, Paleogene sediments dip gently westward. We sampled two sites (IA, IB) in Paleogene red beds and three sites (IC, IR and IS) in Miocene grey to yellowish-grey sediments. At the southern edge of the Talas basin (Talas locality), the bedding dips gently southward. DISCUSSION Timing of Magnetization For most of our samples, demagnetization provided well- determined HTCs, consistent at basin level.The reversal test is also positive for the three basins, as well as the conglomerate test at Dzhety-Ogyuz locality. n of Cenozoic deformation in Central Asia, we studied the paleomagnetism of Tertiary red beds and lava flows from intermontane basins in the Tien-Shan region of Kyrgyzstan. We collected 532 cores and hand samples from 78 sites at 12 localities and progressively demagnetized them, thermally or with alternating fields. For most sites, there are magnetic components with unblocking temperatures higher than 600øC. We infer that the magnetic carriers are mainly hematite and magnetite.
