a Cenozoic right-lateral displacement of 110'!'_60 km on the Talas-Fergana fault. INTRODUCrION Argand [1924] compiled a tectonic map of Eurasia. He inferred that northward motion of India and its subsequent collision (\"affrontement\") with Asia were responsible for Cenozoic reactivation of earlier structures and for anomalous relief throughout much of Central Asia. Recent work has done much to confirm and quantify these ideas. Crustal shortening within Tibet was attributed to reactivation of earlier structures by Dewey and Burke [1973]. Seismicity and studies of fault traces on satellite imagery confirmed the extent of active deformation within Central Asia [Molnar and Tapponnier, 1975]. From magnetic anomalies in the Indian Ocean, India is estimated to have collided with Eurasia about 55 Ma ago [Patriat and Achache, 1984]. Since then, paleomagnetic and structural evidence suggests that there has been a further convergence of about 2000 km between India and Eurasia [Achache eta/., 1984; Savostin et al., 1986]. Still not clear is the style of deformation within Central Asia over the last 55 Ma. Molnar and Tapponnier [1975] drew attention to the importance of strike-slip faulting. Tapponnier et al. ary. Jolivet et al. [1990] suggested that the opening of the Japan Sea was a consequence of counterclockwise rotation of blocks at the northeastern end of the Gulf of Oman-Pamir-Ba'al wrench zone. These fields were chosen so as to evaluate the influence of hematite and goethite for the Z axis, single-domain magnetite for the X axis and low- coercivity magnetite for the Yaxis. Remanent magnetization was measured with either a cryogenic magnetometer (LETI) or a Schonstedt spinner flux gate magnetometer. We isolated characteristic directions of remanent magnetism after progressive thermal demagnetization or alternating field demagnetization, performed with Schonstedt equipment. The algorithm, on which is based the test of McFadden and Jones [1981], was used in three different ways. The Nemegosenda carbonatite consists of a nucleus of alkaline syenite and carbonatite, surrounded by brecciated syenitic rocks [Parsons, 1961; Thurston et al., 1977]. Brecciation, alteration, and recrystallization increase outward to a metasomafic aureole. The Archean gneiss in the aureole shows two fenitization zones. The inner zone is characterized by dehydration and reduction with abundant magnetite, and the foliated outer zone is extensively hydrated and oxidized and rich in hematite. Minor late mafic, porphyry, and carbonatite dikes and carbonatite veins occur in and near the complex. Symons and Garber [1974] carried out a paleomagnetic study of 17 sims in different petrological phases in the complex and its aureole. They reported a normal (N) polarity remanence (D=305 ø, 1=+46ø), whose corresponding paleopole (178øW, 43øN) falls among other N poles on the 1100-1050 Ma Logan loop or Keweenawan track of the APWP [Halls and Pesonen, 1982]. We augmented Symons and Garber's study with eight new sites: NE-1, NE-2 and NE-6 were in alkalic syenite, site 3 was in carbonatite at the nucleus of the complex, sims 4, 49, and 66 were in the contact aureole, and site 5 was in syenitic breccia. The shales display two components of remanence. Component 1 (CI) was the only magnetization direction in the majority of the shales, and the first- removed component in 10 shale specimens. Component 2 (C2) is observed as a single-component remanence with a low (300-400øC) unblocking temperature range in samples from one shale station and as a second- removed component in 10 shale specimens. The mean directions are (declination/inclination) 347o/-04 ø (346ø/-47 ø) in situ (tilt-corrected) for CI and 80ø/-63 ø (135ø/-40 ø) for C2. The pencil slates and well-cleaved slates both display single component remanences. The mean directions are 198ø/-12 ø (201ø/26 ø) for the pencil slates and 199ø/24 ø (225o/54 ø ) for the well-cleaved slates. INTRODUCTION Palcomagnetic results from folded Paleozoic sedimentary rocks in the Appalachians define portions of the Early Paleozoic apparent polar wander path (APWP) for North America [see Van der Voo, 1989]. Recently $tamatakos and Kodama [1991a,b] have evaluated the effects of strain on the remanence of two important red bed units, the Carboniferous Mauch Chunk Formation and the Silurian Bloomsburg Formation. They concluded that the remanence directions of these units are deflected from their original, primary direction by strain reorientation of hematite during folding. Thus the palcopoles previously derived from the more strongly deformed parts of these units do not provide an accurate representation of the Earth's field for the depositional age of these units. Similar deflections of remanence carried also by hematite have been observed in folded sediments from the Alps [Kligfield et al., 1983; Hirt et al., 1986] and from Brittany, France [Cognd et al., 1991]. PALEOMAGNETIC STUDY OF TIlE MARTINSBURG FORMATION Comparison With the North American API We have concluded from magnetite remanence and orientation and from structural geology that the characteristic remanence of the shale is prefolding in age. An independent test of this conclusion can be made by comparing the poles calculated from the characteristic directions of the shale and the reference North American apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the Cambrian- Jurassic, generated from the global paleomagnetic data base using all poles from the stable craton with Q_>3 [Van der Voo, 1990] (Figure 12). The tilt-corrected shale C2 pole lies far from any portion of the APWP. This direction is best defined by the Om22A samples in which the remanence is probably carried by pyrrhotite. On this basis we exclude the shale C2 direction from further consideration. The tilt-corrected shale C 1 pole falls near the lower-middle Silurian and lower Devonian portions of the APWP, which would indicate a possible Silurian to lower Devonian remagnetization in the shales. The two hypothesized B R remanences have very similar directions, and since they are both likely thermochemical overprints, their spectra of coercivities and unblocking temperatures must overlap substantially. The best section of western Taimyr is situated in the middle Syradasay River, on the left bank on the northern flank of a horst-anticline (72.9”N, 84”E). The regional dip of the lava varies from block to block, from northwest to northeast. Dips change from 70-80” at the bottom of the section to practi- cally horizontal at the top. The entire thickness is about 1.7 km (Fig. 2). The section is subdivided on geochemical grounds, with, from bottom to top, three suites being recog- nised: Syradasaysky, Labaksky and Verhnetamsky. The lavas of the Syradasaysky suite belong to the alkali-basalt series and are represented by trachy- basalts (with Ti-augite), subalkaline basalts with a higher content of olivine, and hawaiites. The lowest is the Petroz'avodskian Sandstone Formation which has yielded a K-Ar age (on glauconite) of 1800 Ma (Sokolov 1987). Two basaltic lava flows occur in the upper part of this member. A magnetically shielded furnace (inner residual field < 15 nT) was used for the demagnetization experiments, yhereas AF demagnetization was achieved by using a two-axis tumbler system, housed in a set of Helmholtz coils in order to com- pensate for the Earth's local magnetic field in the laboratory. In this paper we present new palaeomagnetic data for the Lake Onega region. The sections studied comprise quartzites, as well as extrusive and intrusive rocks of Vepsian ( 1900-1650 Ma) and Jatulian (2300-2100 Ma) ages, which represent Svecofennian and Jatulian tectonomagmatic events respectively. Thermal and alternating-field demagnetization experiments reveal the presence of several components of the natural remanent magnetization of normal and reversed polarity. A pilot collection ( 18 samples), representative of all rock types sampled, was subjected to a variety of rock-magnetic experiments at the Institute of Physics of the Earth in Moscow. These experiments include determinations of saturation magnetization J, and saturation remanence J,, as a function of temperature, as well as AF and DC demagnetization of Jrs. In order to improve this situation and to assess the G1 -G5 c 500 0 500m - reliability of the earlier data, a cooperative palaeomagnetic study has been undertaken. Sequences of Lower Proterozoic rocks in the Lake Onega region (both sedimentary and igneous rocks) covering the Vepsian (1850-1650 Ma) and Jatulian (2300-2150 Ma) ages, originally studied by Katzeblin ( 1968), Ignatjeva ( 1974), Khramov & Ignatjeva (1980) and Gooskova & Krasnova (1985), have been resampled. 2 GEOLOGICAL SETTING AND SAMPLING The sampling region lies close to the west and northwest shore line of Lake Onega, in the southeast Fennoscandian Shield (Fig. 1). This region belongs to the Onega depression, which lies on the southeast side of the Karelian tectonic province (Sokolov 1987). The Vepsian (1850-1650 Ma) age sequence comprises two members. The lowest is the Petroz'avodskian Sandstone Formation which has yielded a K-Ar age (on glauconite) of 1800 Ma (Sokolov 1987). Two basaltic lava flows occur in the upper part of this member. However, only a minor portion of the data used for this and for the earlier compilations has been obtained from the eastern part of the Fennoscandian Shield, thus prompting the present study. In this paper we present new palaeomagnetic data for the Lake Onega region. The sections studied comprise quartzites, as well as extrusive and intrusive rocks of Vepsian ( 1900-1650 Ma) and Jatulian (2300-2100 Ma) ages, which represent Svecofennian and Jatulian tectonomagmatic events respectively. Thermal and alternating-field demagnetization experiments reveal the presence of several components of the natural remanent magnetization of normal and reversed polarity. Component A, has been identified in a sill of Vepsian gabbro-dolerites (1770 Ma) exposed at Rybreka locality and yields a palaeopole at 37.8"N, 210.6"E (dp = 4.0", dm = 7.7'). This magnetization is interpreted to be of thermoremanent origin. A pilot collection ( 18 samples), representative of all rock types sampled, was subjected to a variety of rock-magnetic experiments at the Institute of Physics of the Earth in Moscow. These experiments include determinations of saturation magnetization J, and saturation remanence J,, as a function of temperature, as well as AF and DC demagnetization of Jrs. The peak fields used for the latter two experiments reach 100 mT and 2000 mT respectively. In addition, stepwise thermal and AF demagnetization experi- ments were carried out on specimens from the pilot cpllection. A magnetically shielded furnace (inner residual field < 15 nT) was used for the demagnetization experiments, yhereas AF demagnetization was achieved by using a two-axis tumbler system, housed in a set of Helmholtz coils in order to com- pensate for the Earth's local magnetic field in the laboratory. In the case of stronger remanence, continuous thermal demagnetization was carried out in a thermal demagnetizer incorporated in the spinner magnetometer. A pilot collection ( 18 samples), representative of all rock types sampled, was subjected to a variety of rock-magnetic experiments at the Institute of Physics of the Earth in Moscow. In addition, stepwise thermal and AF demagnetization experi- ments were carried out on specimens from the pilot cpllection. Core samples were then distributed among the participating laboratories for standard palaeomagnetic measurements. A pilot collection ( 18 samples), representative of all rock types sampled, was subjected to a variety of rock-magnetic experiments at the Institute of Physics of the Earth in Moscow. These experiments include determinations of saturation magnetization J, and saturation remanence J,, as a function of temperature, as well as AF and DC demagnetization of Jrs. The peak fields used for the latter two experiments reach 100 mT and 2000 mT respectively. In addition, stepwise thermal and AF demagnetization experi- ments were carried out on specimens from the pilot cpllection. A magnetically shielded furnace (inner residual field < 15 nT) was used for the demagnetization experiments, yhereas AF demagnetization was achieved by using a two-axis tumbler system, housed in a set of Helmholtz coils in order to com- pensate for the Earth's local magnetic field in the laboratory. In the case of stronger remanence, continuous thermal demagnetization was carried out in a thermal demagnetizer incorporated in the spinner magnetometer.
